articles.title: A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes
articles.summary: Chefs in the east of the country are shunning imported produce for local ingredients, reinforcing how food is intertwined with a region and its people. ‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses at Högbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm…
body: The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended.

“Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home.

Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the old bruk buildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses.
points: Chefs in the east of the country are shunning imported produce for local ingredients, reinforcing how food is intertwined with a region and its people.

articles.title: Rise of the student commuters: weighing the costs of living at home or in halls
articles.summary: Changing social trends and creative timetables are making it more likely for students to stay at home while they study. Is campus life on the way out? For Lucy Brazier, a second-year business management student, commuting to university was an easy decision.
body: And with overnight accommodation available on campus, she feels she gets the best of both worlds. “I can book a room at less than a day’s notice for £35 so I don’t have to drive home. I’ve used it after nights out, and the evening before exams so I don’t have the stress of driving in the morning. It’s been really helpful.”
Brazier is far from alone. More students are choosing to live at home while studying, and universities are increasingly adapting their courses and campuses to make commuting easier.

According to Ucas, 612,690 UK students aged 18 to 20 who applied before 14 January 2026 made at least one application stating that they intended to live at home – up 8% from last year’s figure of 569,880.

With commuter students now a significant presence on campus, Universities UK chief executive Vivienne Stern says the traditional model of student life is changing. “Universities are evolving to meet the needs of learners. Many offer flexible ways to access learning and resources, or adjust students’ timetables to suit those with longer commutes or other responsibilities.”

articles.title: My partner’s sister has published a family memoir that's unfair to him. Should we cut ties? | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.summary: She should have been much more careful, but everyone has their own version of the ‘truth’. Does your partner want a reconciliation? My sister-in-law wrote and published an emotionally charged “memoir” of family dislocation and trauma, in which she massaged the truth of her family’s past to portray…
body: She tried to de‑identify her brother, but he would be recognisable to anyone with a rudimentary ability to search the internet. Legal action was considered, but decided against. Who gets to tell a story in these times? Whose story is more “true ”? And should we cut off all ties or attempt reconciliation?

You have every right to be aggrieved. This sounds upsetting, unfair and also largely avoidable. Unless your partner’s inclusion was an essential and pivotal part of the book (in which case he may have wanted to write the story himself), I wonder why he was included in a way that could identify him, and why she didn’t give you a heads-up.

But family members don’t always behave in ways we like, and in families there is usually one person who feels they own the narrative and know all the truths. It may feel as if, by putting her account in a book, your sister-in-law has claimed the definitive, “true” version. But that’s just her side of it. Your question about “who gets to tell a story” is pertinent because not everyone will go on to write a memoir, but many people can and do post a mini version on social media.
points: She should have been much more careful, but everyone has their own version of the ‘truth’.
My sister-in-law wrote and published an emotionally charged “memoir” of family dislocation and trauma, in which she massaged the truth of her family’s past to portray…

articles.title: Ketchup on a Sunday roast? This is the worst thing gen Z has ever done | Polly Hudson
articles.summary: Swapping roast potatoes and yorkshire puddings for kimchi and avocado – how can they live with themselves? Trigger warning: the following contains a description of the most heinous abomination known to humankind. Ready? A diabolical 39% of gen Z add ketchup to their Sunday roast.
body: And their misdemeanours do not end there. In news that is particularly distressing on the eve of glorious roast season, it turns out they’re also exchanging roast potatoes and yorkshire puddings for hot sauce, kimchi and – sounds like a punchline, but isn’t – literally avocado.

Sorry, but how dare they? You do not mess with perfection, which is what a roast is – that’s why so many of us choose it for our imaginary death row last meal. It’s comforting, delicious, a ritual and a treat. Peak food. Never mind the audacity of tweaking it at all – the tweaks themselves add insult to injury. The roast potato is the star of the plate, for goodness sake! Substituting it is like taking Meryl Streep out of a movie, and replacing her with … well, an avocado.

Gen Z are also determined to cut off their noses to spite their faces, with a horrifying 14% of them eschewing gravy. This is clearly a travesty. Leaving your roast dry is not allowing it to achieve its full potential, cheating it of fulfilling its destiny. How can they live with themselves?
points: Swapping roast potatoes and yorkshire puddings for kimchi and avocado – how can they live with themselves?

articles.title: Elena Rybakina Wins the US Open Women’s Championship
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina is the freshly crowned US Open women’s champion, beating Aryna Sabalenka, 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in a closely fought match on Saturday.
body: It’s Rybakina’s third major, having won Wimbledon in 2022 and the Australian Open earlier this year.

It’s Rybakina who came out of the gate faster, stronger, and with fewer errors—serving hard and with pinpoint accuracy, and seemingly bloodless in her power and precision on her way to taking the first set 6-4 (hence her sometime nickname on tour, the “Ice Queen”). Sabalenka’s composure, meanwhile, was maybe best expressed by the warning she received early in the first set for ball abuse after sending one high into the crowd in a moment of frustration.

The two had faced each other 17 times before on the tour, with Sabalenka winning 10 of those matches—but they’d been dead even since 2023. Perhaps more crucially, they’d played each other in two Grand Slam finals (both at the Australian Open), with each player winning once.

articles.title: What Happens After the Runway? Inside the Best Post-Show After-Parties of NYFW
articles.summary: Thought the fun ended after the model walk finale? Think again. Here’s Vogue’s peek inside the buzziest after-parties of the Spring 2027 season…
body: Jonathan Simkhai’s Friday night party didn’t take long to get going. Right after his show, the designer traded the runway for the dance floor at Boom at The Standard Hotel. Hosted in partnership with Google Shopping, the gathering saw guests crowded around the bar with St-Germain Hugo Spritzes in hand as Amerie gave a surprise performance of her beloved track, 1 Thing.

Tucked behind Cherry Lane Theatre, the Wild Cherry restaurant buzzed with post-show excitement on Friday evening as guests got together to raise a glass to the enduring relationship between Wiederhoeft and The Webster.

“The Webster is our home in New York City,” Jackson Wiederhoeft told Vogue. Laure Hériard Dubreuil, founder of the luxury retailer, was an early admirer and supporter of the former Vogue /CFDA Fashion Fund finalist. Dressed in a black gown by the designer, she added: “Every single one of Jackson’s creations feels like they are made for you.”

articles.title: Benito Skinner on Embracing “Nasty” Style—and a ’Stache Reveal!—at NYFW
articles.summary: “It takes at least five gay men to get me ready for an event,” says the Overcompensating star, who sat front row at Calvin Klein with his famous bestie Mary Beth Barone.
body: Every New York Fashion Week, is there any show with a more star-studded front row than Calvin Klein? Hm, debatable. Yesterday, as designer Veronica Leoni unveiled her new spring 2027 collection for the label (let’s talk about those chic suits!), the front row was, in typical form, stacked. Rosalia! Katie Holmes! Pam Anderson! But nobody brought the heat quite like Overcompensating star Benito Skinner, sporting a shimmery button-up and gray trench.

“I think I picture a young me, and what he would’ve said if he saw me sitting with my best friend at the Calvin Klein show in New York City,” Skinner tells Vogue the day after the show. (He sat with his bestie and fellow Ride podcaster, Mary Beth Barone.) “We’ve come a long way since sneaking into the underwear department of Dillard’s, and staring at the Calvin Klein underwear boxes.”

articles.title: See the 1972 Vogue Story That Inspired Anna Sui’s Dreamy Spring 2027 Collection
articles.summary: Enchanted by Howard Gardiner Cushing’s paintings, the designer went down a reseach rabbit hole.
body: Editor’s Note: The spring 2027 Wonderment collection Anna Sui presented at the National Arts Club—feaeturitn a fairy-tale print, pretty parasoles, and delicate lingerie looks—has its roots in the pages of Vogue. The designer explained how that came to be in her show notes, writing: “I discovered Howard Gardiner Cushing’s painting s while flipping through a 1970s issue of Vogue, searching for an Avedon photograph of an Ara Gallant hairstyle. On Justine Cushing’s walls were the most fantastical paintings. What began as a search for a photograph suddenly became something else entirely: a new visual world opening before me.”
“An American Fantasy: The Long Island Beach House of Mrs. Justine B. Cushing,” photographed by Horst P. Horst, first appeared in the November 1, 1972 issue of Vogue.

articles.title: 11 National Parks That Are Even More Beautiful in the Fall
articles.summary: Enjoy changing leaves in Shenandoah and cooler days in Big Bend.
body: I’ve traveled far and wide through America’s national parks, and if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that some landscapes are simply better with a little fall color. Come September and October, sweeping valleys turn gold, forests flare in riots of red and pops of orange, and high country trails welcome that crisp, exhilarating drop in temperature that makes you want to keep trekking a little farther. Even parks we know and love in summer feel completely transformed: the sunsets shine differently, wildlife activity changes, and the seasonal crowds begin to give way to a quieter, more immersive experience.

Thanks to the breadth of terrain across the US national parks, there’s no single version of how to experience fall. You might be leaf-peeping beneath the peaks of the Tetons, winding through Acadia’s brilliant coastal forests, hiking Yosemite in the cooler weather, or watching the aspens flicker across the Rockies. And when the sun goes down, the day doesn’t have to end: there are campfires to linger around, stars to seek out, and hot springs to slip into.
